en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Two:
Correctly Clarifying the Manifest Objects, in ten sections: First, Grasping at Causes and What is Caused, in two parts;
first, regarding their understanding.

“Ānanda, you should know that these good men have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned to the source within consciousness; they have already extinguished birth and death, yet their subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.”

Although the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted and the cycle of arising and ceasing has already ceased, consciousness returns to its source yet has not yet attained ultimate quiescence; therefore, it is said that "the essence is subtle and wondrous, but not yet perfected.
This is because consciousness has not yet been shattered, as one is still within the realm of subtle arising and ceasing.
"Exquisite and wondrous" refers to the exquisite, true, and wondrous clarity.

It can cause one's own physical faculties to interpenetrate, merge, open, and close; it also enables universal awareness to commune with all categories of beings throughout the ten directions, such that this pervasive and harmonious awareness can enter the perfect source.
This refers to a momentary state within contemplation.
Although the barriers between the sense faculties appear momentarily to open within this contemplation, they have not yet attained full mutual interchangeability.

As for the "universal awareness of all categories," within this contemplation one perceives that the sentient beings of the ten directions and one’s own body share the same single awakened nature (*ekabuddhatā*), merging with one another such that there is no distinction between their cognitions; this is precisely what constitutes entry into the perfect and fundamental source.
This realm is entirely a reflection of consciousness and has not yet reached quiescence.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "Yet regarding quiescence, its subtle and wondrous essence is not yet perfected.
To establish a cause of true permanence within that which is returned to, and thereby give rise to a superior understanding, is precisely the arising of conceptual attachment.

Regarding the objects of universal awareness entered therein as true and eternal, one establishes them as the cause capable of producing all things; this is then taken as the ultimate refuge, certain and unerring—therefore, it is called "resolute conviction" (adhimukti).
Second, the judgment that they belong to the ranks of heterodox followers:

"Such persons fall into the attachment to causes and their underlying reasons; they become companions of the *puruṣa* and the *pradhāna* (the primal principle) to which the *Kapila* school resorts; they are deluded regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha and have lost their true knowledge and vision."
"This is called the first [type of] establishing a mind that has attained its goal, thereby forming a fruit to which one returns.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of external paths.

Regarding the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the cause, one clings to it as being truly eternal; since it is the cause of all phenomena, it is called "clinging to the cause of causes."

All phenomena are without cause, arising and ceasing in falsehood; yet now you reckon that there is a cause which is of a true and eternal nature. This is no different from the attachments of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who hold that the "Primal Darkness" (mūla-prakṛti) is eternal and capable of producing all things. This is precisely reckoning the primordial state of the ālayavijñāna, before any signs or manifestations had appeared, as being the Primal Darkness.
Regarding "deluded regarding Buddha-enlightenment": enlightenment (*bodhi*) means awakening; the essence of awakening is free from thought.
That which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception, a single mark throughout the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Now, to maintain that phenomena arise from a single cause while there is a distinction between subject and object is what is meant by "delusion.
Because one does not know according to reality, it is called "losing sight of knowledge and vision."

The mind that is attained is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*); it is "that which is attained" within the causal state and "that to which one returns" upon reaching the fruition.
The remainder of the text is intelligible.
Question:
According to the seven subsequent sections, all speak of "the capable" and "the incapable," etc.; why is this particular passage alone identified as the "cause of causes"?
Answer:

Because all phenomena arise from the transformation of consciousness, it is precisely this that constitutes the cause. Because [beings] fail to understand that these are illusory and falsely grasp them as being identical to reality, they are thus the same as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
The following passage directly reveals that the essence itself is false; therefore, it says "not the agent," and so forth.
Second, the attachment to the agent and the non-agent, in two parts:
first, with respect to what is conceptualized.

“Ānanda! Furthermore, if a son of good family has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth-and-death, yet his subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*) is not yet perfected;

if he takes that which he returns to as his own self-essence, and develops a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of space are but a single class flowing forth from within his own body—although his previous calculation still clung to the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the cause of true permanence, he had not yet taken it as his own self-essence.”
Now, calculating this, it is my very own self; all sentient beings emerge from me, and I am able to give birth to them—this is certainly not an error.
Second, [the teaching] is judged to belong to heterodox followers.

"This person then falls into the dualistic grasping of 'ability' and 'inability'; Maheśvara manifests boundless bodies to become their companion, causing them to lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision."
This is called the second [type of] establishing the capacity to function as the mind, thereby accomplishing the fruit of its functional activity.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana; it gives rise to the seeds of the "Greatly Arrogant Heaven" where the self is pervasive and complete.
In reality, that which is not capable of producing [something] is grasped as being capable; this is called "the capable and the incapable.
Maheśvara—that is, Maheśvara, the Great Lord—has three eyes and eight arms; he is the cause of production according to the non-Buddhist schools (tīrthikas).
The manifestation of the Boundless Body (Anantakāya) occurs because, by grasping at a self, one is able to manifest as immeasurable sentient beings.
Since the cause is capable of this, the fruit accomplishes its function; thus, cause and effect correspond to one another.
3. Grasping at permanence and impermanence; this has two parts.
First, regarding their conceptual reckonings:

"Furthermore, good son, you have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and have already extinguished birth and death, yet your subtle and wondrous state of cessation has not yet reached full perfection."

"If one has an object of refuge and relies upon it, yet suspects that one's own body and mind flow forth from it, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it—then regarding the very ground from which everything flows forth as the true, eternal body, one lacks the understanding of non-arising and ceasing. Amidst arising and ceasing, one prematurely calculates a state of permanence; thus, being deluded about non-arising and likewise confused about arising and ceasing, one dwells securely in this deep-seated confusion. As for those who develop such a 'superior resolve' (adhimukti), their object of refuge is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha*. Previously, they viewed the object of refuge as their own self; now, they recognize the object of refuge as an external entity, and therefore suspect that their own bodies and all phenomena arise from it."
That which pervades and flows through all stages is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

To delusively perceive it as being "other," as being real, as being permanent, as being without arising or ceasing, and as being non-delusive, while failing to realize that original enlightenment is eternally abiding and does not give rise to any phenomena, is to be confused and fail to understand.
"Furthermore, those deluded regarding arising and ceasing" falsely perceive the aggregates of consciousness as being truly permanent.
Because they fail to recognize both [the true nature and the false appearance], they are said to be "sunk in delusion.
Because they cling tenaciously and do not turn away from it, it is called "abiding securely."
2. Judgment as belonging to the ranks of heterodox followers:

"Such a person falls into the attachment to permanence and impermanence; they take the Lord Creator (Īśvara) as their companion, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision."
"This is called the third establishment of causes based on the mind to produce delusive conceptualizations of results.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of inverted perfection.
To conceptually construct permanence within what is impermanent is called the "attachment to the permanent within the impermanent."
Īśvara is Maheśvara (Śiva). Previously, he calculated that others were born from himself;
now, he clings to the view that he arises from another. Therefore, it is said that he calculates [the self] as Īśvara.

Because the mind is taken as the basis, it is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Establishing it as a separate entity, one calculates that it can produce the self; therefore, this is the same as the non-Buddhists' calculation that [the self] is eternal.
Fourth, the attachment to knowledge and non-knowledge, in two parts:
first, regarding what is understood.

"Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet has not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).

If, because his knowledge of the objects of cognition is pervasive and perfect, he establishes a conceptual understanding based on that knowledge, such that he regards all grasses and trees in the ten directions as sentient beings no different from humans—whereby grasses and trees become humans, and upon human death they return to becoming grasses and trees throughout the ten directions—if one gives rise to such a superior resolve through indiscriminate, pervasive knowledge," then "the objects of cognition" refers to the *vijñāna-skandha* (aggregate of consciousness), for it is the object of observation known by that contemplative practice.
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is able to transform all phenomena; this is called "knowledge being pervasive and perfect.
Realizing that these phenomena arise from the transformation of knowledge and take knowledge as their essence, it is said that "understanding is established by means of knowledge."

The passage "the grasses and trees of the ten directions" below immediately explains the aspect of practice (*xingxiang*). Since both the environment and its inhabitants (*yi-zheng*) all exist through cognition, how could it be that one part possesses cognition while another part lacks it?
Therefore, there is no discernment;
they know everything and claim with certainty that they are unerring, which is why it is called "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*).
Second, [this view] is judged to belong to heterodox followers.

“Such a person falls into the attachment to knowledge and non-knowledge; they become companions to the Pāṭhas and Sainīyas who cling to all mental perceptions, thereby becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision.”
This is called the fourth calculation, which falsely conceives that the mind achieves the fruit of perfect knowledge.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of inverted cognition.
Since grasses and trees are devoid of cognition yet one clings to them as having cognition, it is said: "clinging to cognition where there is no cognition."
Pāṭha and Śreṇika were two heterodox teachers. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"Pāśita and Śreṇika"—these are slight phonetic variations of the Sanskrit names. Since they maintained the doctrine of universal consciousness (*sarvajñatva*), they held that even grasses and trees possess life.
"Complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) is synonymous with "universal knowledge.

Regarding the "fruition of error," this refers to the refutation of its being a product of deluded thought (*vikalpa*); it means not realizing that all things are transformations of deluded consciousness and the solidification of deluded thought, wherein "insentient things" are falsely established and "sentient beings" are merely provisional names for the movement of deluded thought.
As stated in the preceding text: "Perception crystallizes into the realm; cognition constitutes sentient beings.
Because one does not distinguish between the unreal consciousness and its internal and external aspects, attachment and fixation arise.
5. Grasping at Birth and Non-Birth; Part Two:
One, concerning their conceptual reckonings.

"Furthermore, good son, you have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and have already extinguished birth and death, yet regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected."

"If one has already attained conformity within the interfused mutual functioning of the sense organs, then all things will arise through circular transformation: seeking the light of fire, delighting in the purity of water, loving the circulation of wind, and observing the accomplishment of dust. Each of these is venerated and served; thus, by taking these various sensory objects as the primary cause for their manifestation, one establishes the understanding of permanence. Regarding "attaining conformity within the mutual functioning of the sense organs," it is called "conformity" because one has temporarily attained resonance with a semblance of contemplation.
Regarding "the perfect transformation that gives rise to all": all dharmas are equally termed "transformations," hence it is called "perfect transformation.
Because they can all be cultivated to achieve the fruits of sagehood, it is called "giving rise to all."

Because one may temporarily attain all functions through a single faculty, one knows by this analogy that it is likewise for all others; thus, within ignorance and non-seeing, one can cultivate and achieve knowledge and vision to grasp the fruit of permanence, and therefore seeks fire, delights in water, craves wind, and contemplates dust.
2. Judgment as Belonging to the Heretical Faction:

"This person falls into the attachment to birth within non-birth. Together with the various Kāśyapas and Brahmins who diligently exert their minds and bodies, serving fire and venerating water in their quest for liberation from birth and death, they become his companions. They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision."
This is called the fifth attachment: the veneration of external objects. With a deluded mind following after things, one establishes false causes for seeking and falsely hopes for results.
This is to be far removed from perfect penetration and to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformation.
The nature of the four great elements truly cannot produce an eternally abiding fruit; yet, by clinging to them as being able to produce it, one is said to "cling to the non-arising of arising.

As for those whose deluded minds follow external objects, they lose sight of what is seen as being solely mind and instead each accord with and revere external things in their quest for the eternal. Since both cause and effect are illusory, this constitutes false seeking and false aspiration.
Sixth, clinging to that which has no refuge; this has two parts.
First, regarding their understanding:

"Furthermore, a good son who has exhausted all conditioned phenomena into emptiness and already extinguished arising and ceasing, yet has not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction."

"If one reckons within the perfect luminosity that there is emptiness amidst the light, and—rather than extinguishing the manifold transformations—takes the eternal extinction of the basis as one's refuge and gives rise to resolute conviction: regarding 'emptiness amidst the light,' this refers to the principle of perfect luminosity, which is precisely the consciousness that is the object of contemplation."
Because birth and cessation have already been extinguished, it is clear that the center is void.
Since it is not itself extinction, it is said to be "not extinction.
Form, sensation, perception, and formations encompass all phenomena; these are called the "multitude of transformations."
The "eternal extinction of the basis" refers to the emptiness within the midst of illumination.
This reckoning takes emptiness as the place of ultimate refuge, which is precisely Nirvana.
Second, this is judged to belong to heterodox followers.

“Such a person falls into the attachment of ‘no refuge as their refuge’; they become companions among the Śūnyatas in the Heaven of No-Thought, deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and having lost their true knowledge and vision.”
"This is called the sixth [type of delusion]: the mind of empty voidness and non-existence, which results in the fruit of nihilistic extinction.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of annihilationism.
This clarifies that while the central void is neither real nor a place of refuge, one falsely calculates it as a refuge; hence it is called "clinging to a refuge where there is no refuge."
In the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), for five hundred great kalpas, the mind of perception does not function.
Śūnyatā refers to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
Perfect emptiness is the absence of mind; it is the severance of the cause of extinction.
The fruit of emptiness and loss is the fruit of annihilationism.
Seventh, the attachment to what is not greed as being greed has two parts:
first, concerning that which is reckoned.

"Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected:

if he forms a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that by making his body firm and permanent, it may become identical with the subtle and perfect [essence], remaining forever without decay or passing away—this refers to one who clings to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as being perfect and eternal, desiring to make this body likewise identical to the aggregate of consciousness; therefore, it is said that 'it would be identical to the subtle and perfect, remaining forever without decay or passing away.'"
Second, the judgment that this belongs to the ranks of heterodox followers:

"Such a person falls into the attachment to greed and non-greed; they become companions to those Āsitas who seek long life, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision."
This is called the seventh attachment, clinging to the source of life; it establishes a cause of solid delusion to pursue the fruit of long-term toil.
It violates and distances itself from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of deluded prolongation.
"The physical body composed of the sense organs is illusory and fundamentally impermanent; it truly cannot be craved as something enduring.
Now, because you stubbornly crave and cling to it, falsely grasping at immortality, it is said that 'craving is not craving, but clinging.'"
Asita is called "The Peerless" (Wubi); he is the Immortal of Longevity (Changshou Xian).
Regarding "the fruit of long labor" (chang lao guo), "labor" (lao) means "firmness" (laogu); it is merely an error in the character used.
Because he falsely clung to prolonging his life, it is called "falsely prolonged" (wang yan).
8. Grasping at the Real as Unreal; Part Two:
One, concerning their understanding.

"Furthermore, good sons, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, they have not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction."

"Contemplating that life-force is mutually interpenetrating, yet fearing that one might exhaust the residual dust of worldly toil, one then sits within a Lotus Palace at this juncture, extensively transforming the seven treasures and increasing the number of precious consorts, indulging the mind as one wishes; for those who thus give rise to superior understanding," [it is because] they contemplate the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as the source of life for all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the universal essential of the life-force of the twelve classes of beings. Thus, my life-force penetrates theirs, and their life-force penetrates mine; hence it is said to be "mutually interpenetrating."

Now, if one observes that the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) were to be exhausted, then the lives of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions would be exhausted, and my own life would likewise be exhausted. If all were exhausted, whom could I instruct to realize the principle of true permanence?
Who are those beings to be transformed?

They possess only a semblance of true permanence, yet lack one who realizes the truth; thus they remain amidst worldly toil and, conversely, give rise to craving and desire. They transform lotus palaces and various sensual realms to indulge in pleasure at will, plotting that their lives shall not perish so that they may realize the truth, manifesting activity to transform sentient beings. Because they maintain this fixed attachment and resolve without wavering, it is called "superior understanding" (*adhimukti*).
The "Warmth" (Yuan) is the Woman-Jewel.
Second, the judgment on those belonging to the heterodox faction:
"Such a person falls into the attachment to 'true' and 'untrue'; Takṣaka and Kāla become their companions; they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision."
"This is called the eighth cause: giving rise to false thoughts and establishing the fruit of blazing afflictions.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving birth to the race of celestial Māras.

To give rise to delusions and indulge in desires is truly not the realization of truth; yet, calculating that this very state can realize truth and manifest its functions, one clings to what is not true as being true—hence it is called "clinging to the non-true as true."

The term *Ṭakkirāja* has not yet been seen in a correct translation; since he is able to transform and enjoy objects of desire, he belongs to the class of the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the cause of perverse thought: because one gives rise to this perverse notion while in meditative concentration and fails to examine it skillfully, intense afflictions arise from this; therefore, he is identical to the celestial Māra.
9. Śrāvakas of Fixed Nature: two parts.
First, according to their understanding:
"Furthermore, a good son has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena and has already extinguished birth and death, yet his subtle and wondrous state of cessation is not yet perfected."

Within the clarity of life (*jīvitaprasāda*), they distinguish between the refined and the coarse, and resolve upon the true and the false; yet, while seeking only for cause and effect to correspond through mutual response, they turn their backs on the path of purity—namely, the seeing of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, the realizing of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path—and once dwelling in cessation, they rest there and do not advance further. For those who give rise to such superior understanding, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) becomes manifest; therefore, it is called the "clarity of life."

Since consciousness already contains both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds, we shall now analyze and determine within this context: suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), being contaminated, are termed "coarse" (*audārika*) and "false" (*mṛṣā*); the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*), being uncontaminated, are termed "refined" (*praṇīta*) and "true" (*satya*).

By selecting and discarding the coarse and false aspects of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), while retaining the refined and true aspects of the path (*mārga*) and its cessation (*nirodha*), it is said that one "discriminates between the refined and the coarse.
Taking the cultivation of the path as the stimulus and the realization of cessation as the response, one takes only these; hence it is said that one "seeks only" this.

Regarding "turning one's back on the path of purity": originally, one practiced the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*) wherein the *dharmadhātu* is equal and free from the defilements of the two extremes; this is called the path of purity.
Now, by giving rise to the Hinayana understanding of aversion and aspiration, it is therefore termed "turning one's back."
The term "inferior" explains the meaning of what preceded.
Second, it is judged to belong to the ranks of heterodox followers:

"Such a person falls into the category of those fixed in the stage of the Śrāvaka; they become companions to those arrogant monks who have heard nothing. They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision."
This is called the ninth: the perfectly refined essence that accords with the mind, resulting in the fruit of quiescence.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of being enmeshed in emptiness.

As for those of fixed nature, they are provisionally designated as "fixed" based on their inclination toward quiescence for a single lifetime without change; yet in reality, after a certain number of kalpas, they will ultimately turn back toward the Supreme Vehicle.
Those who have not heard [the Dharma] do not understand the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) and are deluded into mistaking it for nirvana; therefore, they are the same as these [others].

"Complete" (yuan) means all-pervasive, and "refined" (jing) means not coarse; because one has already transcended the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) and serves as the source of all life, it is called "complete refinement" (yuanjing).
Because it accords with false conceptualization, it is said to "correspond to the mind.
Tenth, the pratyekabuddha of fixed nature has two parts:
first, [an explanation] based on what they understand.

"Furthermore, good son, having exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, one’s state of tranquil extinction has not yet reached ultimate perfection.

If, regarding the profound and subtle nature of the perfectly interfused, pure, and luminous awakening, one develops a deep investigation and establishes it as *nirvāṇa* without proceeding further, thereby giving rise to a superior conviction (*adhimukti*), then—taking the originally perceived essence of perfectly interfused, pure, and luminous awakening and now seeing that the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is free from the birth-and-death of conditioned phenomena—one deems this state to be both profound and subtle, and establishes it as *nirvāṇa*."
Because they do not know how to flow and circulate, they do not advance.
Second, it is judged that they belong to the ranks of heterodox followers:

"Such persons fall into the category of those fixed in the nature of Pratyekabuddhas; they become companions to those solitary practitioners who do not resolve to turn their minds [toward enlightenment]. They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision."
This is called the tenth fruit of the perfectly enlightened mind becoming tranquil and luminous.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana; it gives rise to the seed of the unchanging perfect clarity of enlightenment.
To perceive the aggregates as perfect enlightenment is to accord with deluded conceptualization as the harmonious mind.
It is quiescent and unmoving, yet not devoid of cognitive awareness; therefore, it is called "tranquil clarity."

Having realized the perfect luminosity of consciousness-awakening and possessing the wondrous function of non-dual transformation, it is said that they do not transform the seeds of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The śrāvakas have the obstacle of fearing suffering; the pratyekabuddhas have the obstacle of abandoning birth."
This is of that category.
Third, the conclusion and exhortation to propagate and proclaim [the teaching] has four parts:
first, concluding the preceding section and censuring the failure.

“Ānanda! These ten kinds of *dhyāna* may lead to madness midway through their practice due to delusion; one falsely perceives fulfillment within what is not yet fulfilled. All of these arise because the mind of the *vijñānakāya* (consciousness aggregate) is in a state of mutual conflict, and thus this stage is produced.”

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not examine themselves. When encountering these [visions] appearing before them, each rests in their own cherished, previously habituated, and deluded mind, regarding it as the ultimate ground of refuge and peace. They claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed bodhi, thereby committing a great falsehood. At the end of the karma induced by such external paths and demonic influences, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not achieve further progress.

As for those who become insane midway, they are still at the stage of semblance-enlightenment and have not yet attained non-retrogression; because false wisdom arises within them, it is said that they "become insane."

Failing to examine the subtle arising and ceasing of the aggregates of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one falsely claims to have attained realization; therefore, it is said that this is due to reliance on delusion and so forth.
The remainder of the text is easily understood.
Second, the exhortation to propagate and proclaim [the teaching].

"You all should maintain your resolve to uphold the Way of the Tathāgata, and after my parinirvāṇa, transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand its meaning. Do not allow them to encounter Māras or create deep calamities for themselves; protect and comfort them with compassion, neutralize their deviant conditions, and cause their bodies and minds to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that from the very beginning they may achieve fulfillment and never encounter a forked path."
I earnestly exhort future generations: know that as long as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is not yet exhausted, these ten states will manifest their characteristics.
If you recognize them and remain vigilant, the demons will naturally subside;
if you are deluded and grasp at them with attachment, you will inevitably fall into partiality and heterodoxy.
"Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to realizing the stage of truth.
"From the very beginning of cultivation" refers to the fulfillment of the fruition.
"Not encountering byways" means that in the interim there are no further devious or circuitous phases.
These are precisely the ten categories mentioned above.
Third, it reveals that which the Buddha rides upon:

"Such Dharma-gates were previously, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, mounted by Tathāgatas as many as motes of dust, who, through this mind, attained awakening and realized the Unsurpassed Way."
"There is not a single Buddha who has attained Bodhi without destroying the five aggregates; all are able to awaken to them, and thus avoid the forked path.
Fourth, the function of the exhaustion of the aggregates."

"If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then your present sense-faculties will function interchangeably; from this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom.

This "mutual functioning of the present faculties" refers to the previously mentioned third gradual stage, the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), as has already been seen in the preceding text.

Regarding those who enter the stage of Dry Wisdom through the mutual functioning [of the sense organs]: this very mutual functioning constitutes having already entered the stage of Dry Wisdom, for mutual functioning is itself the state of mastery.

As stated in the preceding text: "When the flow is reversed and returns to its entirety as one, the six faculties cease their activity; even unto the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas manifest within it, and this person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

From this point, one gradually cultivates according to the practices undertaken, thereby establishing the stages of the sages; this is called the third gradual sequence of progressive cultivation. Thus, from the stage of Dry Wisdom up to Equal Enlightenment, all are established without departing from this third gradual sequence.
Now, by proceeding from the general to the specific, it is said that one enters from within the mutual functions.
As for the term "Vajra," it is because this practitioner, from beginning to end, achieves accomplishment solely through the cultivation of the Vajra Samādhi.

Therefore, the preceding text states: "These various stages are all purified through cultivation and realization by means of the ten profound parables of diamond-like contemplation as being like an illusion; within *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of the Tathāgatas to gradually penetrate deeper."

Alternatively, this may refer to those of sharp faculties who, upon reaching the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*), exert their minds to bring about transformation, thereby transcending the causal stages and entering directly into Wondrous Enlightenment; thus, they receive the distinct title of "Vajra."
If one is of dull faculties, they must pass through various stages according to their initial practice; therefore, such a person does not receive the name "Vajra," but is merely called "Dry Wisdom."

If this stage is established as the mind immediately following Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is as stated in the preceding passage: "The Tathāgata flows against the current, while the Bodhisattva proceeds along with it until the boundaries of enlightenment intersect; this is called Equal Enlightenment."
"How could one establish the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi) anew upon entering into that [state]?

The ancients were deluded by this and established an additional stage of Vajra-Dry-Wisdom after Equal Enlightenment; this truly misleads later students, as it lacks both logical principle and scriptural precedent, and I dare not accept such a view."

"The perfectly bright and refined mind manifests and transforms within it, like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli. In this way, one transcends the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the four stages of preparatory application, the ten vajra grounds traversed by Bodhisattvas, and the perfect brightness of Equal Enlightenment; thus entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, one fulfills Bodhi and returns to the state of non-attainment."

Once the state of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā*) has been realized as perfectly subtle and wondrous, this mind-nature suddenly gives rise to all practices and suddenly possesses all virtues; hence it is called "arousing transformation.

The wisdom-mind is like lapis lazuli, the causal practices are like jewels, and the resultant virtues are like the moon. This metaphor illustrates how the infinite is manifested within the one, and the one is manifested within the infinite; since the causal practices and resultant virtues are simultaneously complete, they are unhindered, perfect, and luminous—thus, it is like lapis lazuli containing jewels and the moon within.
Regarding "transcending the cause to enter the fruit": because the causes and fruits of transformation were previously initiated and fully realized, one is thus able to transcend.

Because merit is sufficient, it is called the "Ocean of Adornments"; because wisdom is sufficient, one perfects Bodhi; because principle is ultimate, one returns to non-attainment, which is the great Nirvana of eternal quiescence and non-attainment. This refers to those of the lowest capacity who are nonetheless sharp in the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Because it is of inferior grade, one only attains entry into the stage upon the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Because it is again sharp, one may, through the manifestation of transformation therein, transcend all stages.

Now that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, for what reason do you say "transcendence"?
Answer:
The previous explanation was given concerning those of superior faculties who are slightly dull; by analogy, there should likewise be those who attain sudden transcendence.
The present explanation is given concerning those of inferior faculties who are sharp; therefore, it can be said that they transcend.
For example, as previously discussed regarding regression, there should likewise be those who progress through the stages of sainthood; these cases merely appear in different sequences.

I. Response to the Deluded Conception, three parts:
A. General Explanation, two parts:
1. Revealing the Perfect Purity of True Awakening.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The subtle, true, wondrous clarity is fundamentally enlightened, perfect, and pure; it does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements. "Subtle and true" refers to the Dharma-body.
"Wondrous clarity" is *prajñā* (wisdom).
"Perfect purity" is *vimukti* (liberation).
These three virtues are perfectly interfused as the single original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
Birth and death are the path of suffering;
defilements are karma and afflictions.
This, then, is the wondrous nature, perfectly luminous, transcending all names and marks.
II. Clarifying the Arising of False Conceptions, in three parts:
A. Sequentially Narrating the Arising of Delusion:
"Even up to empty space, all are produced by false conceptions."

"This is the original, fundamental, wondrously luminous, and true essence of awakening; through delusion, it gives rise to the various vessel-worlds, just as Yajñadatta mistook his own head for a reflection.
It does not further detail the threefold continuity of matter and mind, hence the phrase "and so forth" (乃至).
If even unconditioned space is but a false manifestation, how much more so are all conditioned phenomena, which exist only due to madness and delusion and are thus like the recognition of a shadow?
Second, the refutation of the false cause has three parts:
first, demonstrating the absence of a cause.
"Delusion has no fundamental cause; it is within the state of delusive thought that the nature of causes and conditions is established.
Since it is called "delusion," how could it have a cause?
If it had a cause, it would not be called delusion; therefore, it is said to be without cause.

Since various false imaginings arise from one another in mutual dependence, giving rise to further delusions and serving as seeds for each other, it is said that the nature of causes and conditions is established within false imagination.
2. Refuting the Attachment to Difference.

"Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call things 'spontaneous' (*svabhāva*). That nature of space likewise arises as a real illusion; both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings."

To speak of "having causes and conditions" is still a false attachment; to further recognize [existence] as spontaneous is to accompany one's delusion. Therefore, it is said that sentient beings' deluded minds engage in conceptualization.
3. Conclusion and Rebuttal.
“Ānanda! When one knows where delusion arises, one speaks of the causes and conditions of delusion.

If delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then speaking of the causes and conditions of delusion would be fundamentally non-existent; how much more so for those who, lacking such knowledge, speculate that it is natural?”
"If one knows that [phenomena] arise falsely, one may allow for the explanation of causes and conditions;
but if the false has fundamentally no arising, whom does one speak of as having causes and conditions?
Even causes and conditions are established within the realm of the false—how much more so when, not knowing they are false, one speculates that they are spontaneous?"
3. Conclusion on Delusive Thought.
"Therefore, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the fundamental cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but delusive thought.
The causes of the five aggregates are originally bound together by falsehood; this establishes the nature of causes and conditions within delusive thought itself.

This nature of causes and conditions is provisionally established within the midst of delusion, intending to lead one to realize that phenomena are fundamentally non-existent; therefore, it is likewise termed "a single false conceptualization.
Second, the specific manifestation has five parts:
first, form (*rūpa*).
"Your body was originally caused by the perception of your parents to arise; if your mind were not perception, you would be unable to come into this state of perception to transmit your life-force.
This specifically refers to perception (*saṃjñā*).

This body is formed by grasping the physical remains of the parents; since those remains are themselves the outflow of conceptualization and craving, it is said that "the parents give birth through conceptualization.
Your entry into the womb likewise occurred through conceptualization and craving, for you took those remains as a superior object of perception.
Consciousness immediately proceeds toward that [womb], coalescing to form the embryonic matrix; therefore it is said, "Your mind is not non-perception, yet it does not come to transmit life.
This, then, is the formation of this physical body through the conjunction of the delusions of the three locations.
"As I previously said:
when the mind conceives of the taste of vinegar, saliva flows from the mouth; when the mind conceives of climbing a high peak, the soles of the feet tingle with acid.

Though the precipice does not exist and the sour object has not arrived, your body is certainly not of the same category as empty falsehoods; how then could the saliva in the mouth emerge simply because of speaking of vinegar?"
This citation serves to introduce and establish the preceding explanation; it specifically cites the passage refuting the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Although the precipice and the sour object do not both reach the body, through what you imagine, they are able to produce the acid water in your mouth and feet.
If it were not for the similarity of deluded thoughts, how could there be the arising of water and the like?
"Tong-lun" (通倫) means "of the same kind.
Therefore, you should know that this manifested physical body of yours is called the first deluded thought of solidity.
This concludes the establishment of the name.
Judging by this, how could it not be "non-perception"?
Therefore, one should know that when deluded thoughts coalesce and solidify, they constitute the aggregate of form; hence it is called "solidity."
2. Feeling (*vedanā*).

"Regarding what has just been said: the mind that conceives of heights can cause your body to truly experience sourness and astringency; this arises from feeling as its cause and is able to move the physical form."

"That which you now experience as the present alternation between what is favorable and beneficial and what is adverse and harmful, and which drives you about, is called the second deluded thought, 'empty luminosity.

The first four lines trace back to the previous notion of the movement of the body within the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), thereby clarifying that the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is likewise a deluded thought.

This is explained through the following reasoning: because one conceives of things such as plums, there arises the experience of receiving them; if it were not a reception, how could water be produced?
This reception is also a transformation of deluded thought, for it is through delusion that the reception arises.

Second, as for "driving about": it refers to leading these phenomena of suffering and pleasure arising from favorable and adverse conditions, thereby resulting in harm or benefit, and being driven by them.
Because it perceives objects and leads [the mind] while being empty, penetrating, and unobstructed, it is called "empty clarity."
Third, perception (*saṃjñā*).

"It is by means of your thoughts and deliberations that you cause your physical body to act; yet the body is not of the same category as thought. For what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
By taking on various forms and images, the mind gives rise to physical manifestations, which correspond to thought."

"When awake, there is the mind of ideation; when asleep, there are various dreams. Thus, your mental ideations, restless movements, and deluded sentiments are called the third false imagination, 'interfusion.
The first two phrases provide the heading: 'thought' refers to ideation (*saṃjñā*); that the body and mind are driven and employed is entirely the work of ideation."
The first part, "The body is not [the cause]," is a refutation of the lower [view].
The first three phrases are a counter-interrogation: if it were not of the nature of perception (*saṃjñā*), how could it follow upon recollection?

The latter five phrases, beginning with "various," correctly reveal [the truth]: whenever one apprehends an external object, one must first form a mental image (*pratibimba*), and only thereafter does the body follow it.
If perception were real, why would it need to be grasped through form?
If form were not perception, it could not move of its own accord.
Since these two depend upon one another, are they not both illusory?
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] is associated with thought.
Although waking and sleeping differ, both are constituted by ideation (*saṃjñā*).
Since sleep already results in dreams, and dreams are not real, one should know that how could the ideation of the waking state possibly be real?
Thus, your subsequent conclusion is this:
one knows that present imaginings and thoughts arise precisely because they are stirred by deluded feelings; how could this not be delusion?
It fuses material substance, permeates mental activity, transforms objective images, and constitutes dreams; therefore, it is called "pervasive delusive imagination."
Fourth, the movement [of time]:
"The principles of transformation do not abide; they shift secretly and incessantly.
Nails grow and hair sprouts; vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles."
"Day and night they alternate with one another, yet there is never any awakening"—this reveals the characteristic of activity (*saṃskāra*).
The first two phrases provide the heading: the *saṃskāra-skandha* flows and migrates; because it is subtle and difficult to perceive, it is said to "not abide, shifting secretly."
The following is the detailed explanation: the first three phrases explain "non-abiding," while the final phrase reveals "secret shifting.
"Ānanda! If this were not you, how could its substance undergo change?"
"If it were truly real, why would you have no awareness of it?
Thus, your various mental formations (saṃskāras) ceaselessly flow from moment to moment; this is called the fourth deluded thought, which is subtle and hidden.
This demonstrates its falsity.
"True" means real. If the aggregate of formations were not your own substance, how could it succeed one another without ceasing?
Furthermore, if it were truly your body, why would you not perceive its arising and ceasing?"
It is not that you cannot [perceive it], but rather that you have no basis for doing so; thus, one knows it to be illusory.
Therefore, as for the names of the subliminal perceptions you have listed below, they shift subtly and are difficult to perceive; hence, they are said to be "profoundly hidden."
5. Consciousness (vijñāna) has two parts:
first, the formal definition of its characteristics.

"Furthermore, that which you call 'constant'—the place where your clarity and brilliance are profoundly still and unshaken—is none other than seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the body. This passage cites and points to the substance of consciousness itself.
The first three phrases cite the [erroneous] conception.

That which the practitioner identifies as subtle and clear, free from the arising and ceasing of formations, steadfastly immovable, and designated as "permanently abiding," is precisely the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*).
"In 'the body,' I am pointing to its physical substance; how could the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing?
This refers to its function.

If it were truly pure and real, it would not tolerate the cultivation of delusion; for what reason, then, did you all once in years past behold a strange object, which for many years you neither remembered nor forgot, yet later, upon suddenly beholding that same anomaly again, your memory was as vivid as before, with nothing lost?"
"Then, within this essence that is lucid, profound, and unshakable, there are moment-to-moment impressions being infused; what calculation can there be?
This precisely reveals the nature of delusion.
The first two phrases are a counter-indication.
If this profound clarity were the true nature (*dharmatā*), it would not be capable of containing false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Habitual tendencies are, in other words, seeds (*bīja*).
The following nine phrases provide a sequential explanation of why this is so.
Regarding "neither recollection nor forgetfulness": if there were recollection at the outset, there would be a time of forgetting;
since there was originally no recollection, forgetfulness is not mentioned.

As for "re-examining," this means seeing again; since there is nothing left out upon seeing again, one can see that this [state] merely accommodates delusive habits. Thus, we know that what is false is not the true, profound clarity.

This concludes the preceding section by way of summary: the perfuming of seeds, the maintenance of those seeds, and the arousal of active manifestations flow on in a stream of arising and ceasing that cannot be calculated.
Second, the subtle and minute nature is further elucidated.

"Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the true reality; it is like a rapid torrent of water that appears tranquil at a glance, yet because the current is so swift it is not perceived, though it is not that there is no flow."
"If it were not for the fundamental source of perception, how could one undergo these deluded habit-energies?
Unless your six faculties function in mutual interchange—whether combined or separated—this false conceptualization will never cease.
This precisely reveals the subtle [nature of the afflictions].
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is detached from mental formations (saṃskāra), and is therefore called "tranquil.
Yet, because it is not eternally abiding, it is said to be "not true.

The metaphor of the "swift current" means that ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not perceive it at all; even those prior to the ten stages (bhūmi), though they have some awareness, do not exhaust it. Thus, it is said that the current flows so swiftly that it cannot be seen.

The phrase "if it were not the source of perception" (*na cet saṃjñā-mūla*) clarifies that this is precisely the root of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), as the eighth consciousness serves as the basis for the realms of existence, destinies, and births.

The four lines beginning with "it is not yours" clarify that [this root] is difficult to sever. Regarding "mutual use," "combination," and "separation": because they manifest by relying on the sense organs, they are termed "mutual use."
"Opening" means to allow for no separation; "closing" means to become a single entity.
As the preceding text states: "When the flow is reversed and returns to the One, the six functions cease.
Opening is itself closing; therefore, there is no duality or distinction between them.
If one does not realize the Truth, this affliction will be difficult to extinguish.

"Therefore, within your present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, there is a habitual practice that, though profoundly clear, is internally formless and void; it is the subtle, refined conceptualization of the fifth inversion."
It is named "subtle" because it is so refined.

Among all the consciousnesses, this is the essential point of habitual conditioning; it is also called the place where the spirit is lucid and profoundly still, hence it is described as "profoundly clear," which refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
It exists yet appears as if non-existent; therefore, it is called "Wangxiang" (Formless Phantom).
"Wang" means non-existence;
"xiang" means semblance.
Because it possesses no physical form or substance, it is called "void and non-existent.
Compared to the preceding aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), this is the most subtle; thus, it is repeatedly described as "subtle and refined.
Third, the summary.
“Ānanda! These five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*) are constituted by five kinds of false conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

These five are the very dharmas experienced as retribution by sentient beings; therefore, they are collectively termed ‘clinging’ (*upādāna*), and are also called the ‘five aggregates of clinging,’ because sentient beings grasp these as their own self.”
2. Answering the question regarding the limit:
"If you now wish to know the depth and shallowness of the causal realms," this answers the question as to what constitutes a realm (*dhātu*).
A realm has the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) and also the meaning of "portion" (*bhāga*).
Because they are distinguished by their causal bases and realms (*dhātu*) and have distinct boundaries, they are called "causal realms.

"Only form and space are the limits of form": here, "form" refers to shape-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) and "space" refers to manifest-color (*vyañjana-rūpa*); both are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Because false form and false emptiness manifest in mutual dependence, the brief mention of form and emptiness encompasses everything exhaustively.
"Only contact and its cessation are the limits of sensation"; contact may be adverse or favorable, thereby constituting the two sensations of suffering and pleasure.
"Free from both opposition and compliance, there is only the single feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

'Only recollection and forgetting are the limits of perception (*saṃjñā*')": whether it be memory or forgetfulness, the grasping of images and the clinging to objects of focus are both simply the boundaries of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)."

"Only cessation and arising are the limits of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). The flux of arising and ceasing consists of the four characteristics of each moment; thus, all that arises and ceases belongs to the category of formations.
"Profound stillness enters and merges with profound stillness, returning to the limit of consciousness.
This profound stillness precedes the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha); merging and returning, it belongs to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
Seeing that consciousness is unmoving, one takes this to be true stillness.
This is designated as the limit of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Because one perceives that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing, and that apart from the state of arising and ceasing there must be profound stillness and tranquility, this very point of cultivation constitutes the boundary of consciousness.
3. Response on Sudden and Gradual:

“These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession; their arising is caused by consciousness, and their cessation proceeds from the elimination of form. This answers the previous question regarding the sudden, while the process of elimination constitutes the gradual exhaustion.

In their arising, they proceed from the subtle to the coarse and from the internal to the external, because all phenomena are transformations of consciousness alone; thus it is said that "arising exists by virtue of consciousness.

In their cessation, however, it proceeds first from the coarse to the subtle and from the external to the internal, just as when washing clothes or polishing a mirror, the coarse impurities fall away first.

However, at the time of their arising, they are not actually sequential; rather, there is an instantaneous transformation within a single thought-moment, and it is only in terms of coarse and subtle aspects that such a description is made.
Likewise, in the contemplative method of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuantun), severance is not gradual; when the practice reaches completion, it occurs naturally in this manner.
"Principle is realized all at once, and through this realization, [delusions] are eliminated simultaneously;
phenomena are not removed all at once, but are exhausted through gradual stages.

This previous passage concerns the arising and severing [of delusions], and such is the logical principle. If one were to definitively hold this interpretation alone, how could one know what is false?

Therefore, one must first attend to principle and subsequently to phenomena, realizing sudden enlightenment while gradually eliminating delusions; only then will the meaning of cultivation and realization be fully understood.
Regarding "sudden enlightenment of principle": if we speak in terms of realizing the perfect principle, then all is severed at once, with no sequence of before or after.

As stated in the preceding text: "Once a single faculty returns to its source, the six faculties achieve liberation; defilements vanish in a single thought, and one attains perfect, luminous, pure, and wondrous clarity.
This realization is likewise so; as the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To know that things are illusory is to leave them; to leave the illusory is to awaken; there is no gradual progression."

Since all dharmas arise from the mind through the production of deluded thoughts, and thought itself is non-thought, everything is suddenly exhausted; because within the true nature there is fundamentally no delusion, it is said that "through awakening, everything is simultaneously extinguished."

Regarding the statement that "affairs are not eliminated instantaneously but are exhausted through successive stages": the delusory dharmas of the five aggregates are termed "affairs. Since these aggregates differ in their coarseness and subtlety, it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that the coarse ones are eliminated first. Although the practice of understanding and cultivation may be sudden, the actual severance proceeds in a fixed order. The rising of the sun and the birth of a child are both metaphors for this principle.
"I have already shown you the knots of the *kalpavṛkṣa* cloth; what is it that you do not understand that you must inquire about this again?
This cites the previous discourse on the knots to rebuke [Aniruddha] for his failure to comprehend them.
As the preceding text states: "The substance of the cloth is the same, yet it becomes different due to knots.
It further states: "From ultimate sameness, ultimate difference arises. And again:
"The six knots share the same substance, yet they are not tied at the same time; when they are untied, how can they be removed simultaneously?"
"In all these cases, while the principle is realized instantaneously, phenomena are not eliminated instantaneously; why then do you ask again?
The relationship between sudden and gradual realization and cultivation is as explained in the *Commentary on the Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué shū*)."
3. Conclusion and Exhortation to Propagate.

"You should take this root-source of deluded thought and cause your mind to attain thorough understanding; transmit it to all practitioners of future ages during the Dharma-ending period, so that they may recognize what is false and vain, develop a deep weariness with their own arising [of afflictions], know that there is nirvana, and no longer cling to the three realms."

As stated above, these five kinds of false conceptualization are the very root of the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Since the five aggregates encompass all phenomena (*dharma*), all phenomena are therefore nothing but false conceptualization.

As stated above: "The Sahā world, together with all impure lands and sentient beings throughout the ten directions, are all equally this awakened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind. Through the conditions of the delusory illness of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they falsely arise through conjunction and falsely die through conjunction."
Since you have realized this, it is said that "the mind has attained opening and penetration.
Furthermore, because you enable others to understand, it is said that you "transmit and show so as to cause them to recognize" it.

If one knows that both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as self and other, are all but a single delusive thought, then one can come to loathe the very substance of the five aggregates and seek to attain the eternal bliss of Nirvana; how could one then still cherish the three realms?

Therefore, this exhortation to propagate [the teaching] benefits both oneself and others. III. First, the raising of the topic that the merit of giving is boundless, in two parts:
first, the question regarding its abundance. "Ānanda!..."

Furthermore, if there were someone who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures to their full capacity, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them without a single thought being in vain;
"What do you think? Would this person, by virtue of the cause and condition of giving to the Buddha, obtain much merit?
This passage performs a comparative calculation (*tulana*).
Although the text is not extensive, its meaning is already complete.
The seven treasures represent the excellence of wealth;
filling the void represents the excellence of abundance;
and the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust represent the excellence of the field of merit.
To serve and make offerings without wasting even a single moment is the excellence of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding space and precious jewels, it is the vast mind.
To offer up to all Buddhas and serve them with offerings is the foremost mind.
The mind is not spent in vain; this is the long-term mind.
Thus, as the practice of spreading and revolving [the offerings] excels both in objective field and mental state, the merit obtained is truly vast!
Second, the answer regarding excellence.
Ānanda replied, "Space is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless.
In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to the Buddha; even after casting off his body, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King."

How much more so when the present space is exhausted and the Buddha-fields are filled, all bestowed with precious jewels such that even contemplating them for an entire kalpa cannot reach their limit—how could there be any boundary to such merit?
By offering seven coins to the Buddha, one attains the rank of a Wheel-Turning King; this demonstrates that among all fields of merit, the merit of the Buddha is supreme.
The merit of a Wheel-Turning King is such that he possesses the seven treasures and is surrounded by a thousand sons.

How much more so when one offers all the rare treasures filling the void to the Tathāgata! The objects thus bestowed would exhaust even an inconceivable number of kalpas, so how could there be any limit to the merit they attract?
None but one possessed of omniscience can know this!
2. Revealing the Superiority of the Sūtra’s Benefits, in two parts:
A. The Gateway of Manifesting Merit through the Transformation of Karma by the Speaker.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"The speech of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is not false"—this declaration is not in vain, so as to inspire deep faith that what the Buddha has spoken is true.

"Furthermore, if there is a person who commits the four grave offenses or the ten *pārājika* transgressions, in an instant they shall pass through the Avīci hells of this world and other worlds, until they have exhausted the entirety of the ten directions of unrelenting suffering, experiencing them all without exception."
This demonstrates that the person has committed the ultimate offense.
*Pārājika* is here translated as "abandonment" (*qi*) or "that which is not to be enjoyed" (*bukeli*).
Because of this abandonment, one is immediately deprived of the utility of the Sangha; because it is not to be enjoyed, one shall enter hell.

If one commits all four *pārājika* offenses of the Hīnayāna or all ten grave offenses of the Mahāyāna, the retribution received will be endless; therefore, throughout the ten directions, there is nowhere they do not reach.
Avīci refers to the five *ānantarya* hells.

"To be able, with a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), to reveal and teach this Dharma-gate to those who have not yet studied during the final age" indicates that the time for propagating the sutra is brief.
A "single thought-moment" is the limit of the mind.
Now, one who extensively propagates the sutras must necessarily do so for a long duration; how could there be anyone who proclaims them in a single thought-moment?
Herein, to manifest the great power of propagating the sutras, the minimum possible time is cited to demonstrate its extraordinary excellence.

"The karmic obstacles of such a person shall be extinguished at the very thought [of this teaching], and the causes for the suffering of hell they are destined to undergo shall be transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss.
This refers to the superiority of the destruction of sin.

Even for one who has committed grave offenses, the power of reciting this sutra for a single moment can overturn the most severe retribution of suffering and transform it into the retribution of Ultimate Bliss.
"The merit obtained shall surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million billionfold; indeed, it is such that even calculation and analogy cannot reach it."
"The merit obtained is supreme!
The previous merit of giving was already difficult to measure, yet this present [merit] now exceeds it by thousands of millions of billions of times, beyond the reach of analogy.
How can it be so wondrous!"
Question:
For a person who has committed the most grievous sins, to preach the Dharma for even a very short duration is not yet sufficient to be called praiseworthy.
Why is it that their karma is extinguished and such extraordinary merit is obtained?
Answer:
There are many reasons why one obtains this superior retribution:
first, the sutra that one propagates is the Buddha’s ultimate discourse, for its teaching, principle, practice, and fruit are all inconceivable.

This means that it reveals how the Tathāgatagarbha and the mind-nature are such that all phenomena—whether sentient or insentient, possessing nature or lacking nature—equally attain the Buddha-way; this principle is inconceivable.

The Buddha-Topknot Heart Mantra allows both those on the path of cause and those who have attained the fruit to rely upon this Dharma to extinguish evil and give rise to good, entering into principle to transform others, warding off the heterodox and protecting the orthodox, advancing with ever-increasing speed, and being able to achieve Bodhi; this teaching is inconceivable.
Among the twenty-five sages of the Perfect Practice Gate, Avalokiteśvara is supreme; this practice is inconceivable.

The third stage among the sixty stages of the sages is the gradual realization of non-arising; it further states that through "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā), one can transcend the causal stages and enter directly into the ocean of fruition—this fruition is inconceivable.
Second, because it is truly rare to be able to propagate this ultimate discourse during such a degenerate age replete with obstacles, while possessing authentic faith and understanding.
Third, the merit of giving yields only the retribution of saṃsāra and remains merely self-benefiting;

whereas the benefit of propagating the Dharma of the sutras can reach the state of outflowlessness (anāsrava), enabling those who hear it to attain unerring faith and understanding, thereby providing inexhaustible benefit and joy as it is transmitted from one to another.
Thus, although a single thought-moment is brief, its benefit is vast!
For this reason, it surpasses the merit of the aforementioned gift of jewels.
Second, the gate of wisdom that reveals the fruit attained by one who upholds [the teaching].
“Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra, my extensive explanation of them would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
Relying on my instructions and practicing the path according to the teaching, they will directly attain Bodhi without further demonic interference.”

Regarding the statement that "a full exposition would not be exhausted," it refers to the preceding passage which says: "If I were to speak this *Siddhārtha* (悉怛多) mantra of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa-Flame, its sounds would continue from dawn until dusk without interruption, and even if the syllables and phrases were not repeated, one could not finish it even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
This demonstrates that both the meaning of the sutra and the merit of its upholder are immeasurable.
By relying on me, one can attain the most ultimate fruit and remain free from internal and external demonic obstacles; thus, it serves as an exhortation to practice according to what has been taught.
This is what those who extensively uphold this sutra attain and from what they are freed; only a Buddha and a Buddha can know this.
Second, the great assembly, having heard with reverence, withdrew after paying their respects.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra—

The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world; as well as the bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, and holy rishis from other directions; together with the powerful spirits and ghosts who have first resolved to attain enlightenment—all were filled with great joy, paid their respects, and departed.
Although the twenty-five sages and Mañjuśrī each have their own expositions, the merit belongs to the Buddha; thus, they are collectively termed "the Buddha's teaching.
As for the three kinds of worlds, it is therefore said that these are the environments in which all vessel-worlds abide.
The Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles are subsumed within the wisdom of perfect enlightenment;
all others belong to the world of sentient beings. The "Holy Sage Youth" is one among this assembly of sages.

Within the sutra there is this mantra: "Great Joy. This refers to attaining worldly joy in the near term and supramundane joy upon reaching the first bhūmi in the distant term. One rejoices for three reasons: [the realization of the Dharma, the attainment of the fruit, and the fulfillment of the purpose].
First, the purity of the person who teaches;
second, the purity of the Dharma taught;
third, the purity of the fruit attained.
Because of this meaning, all were greatly rejoiced.
He concluded with a verse, saying:
"By means of this small portion of praise for the power of the sutra, I bestow it upon others so that its circulation may flow on without end."
All the benefit and happiness obtained is dedicated toward awakening, the limit of reality, and the realm of sentient beings.

On the first day of the New Year in the year of Yisi (1249) during the Chunyou era, Shen Yuansheng of Qinghu respectfully records: The text of the "Seven Manifestations and Eight Arguments" is truly the Tathāgata’s direct pointing to sentient beings regarding the essential method for attaining Buddhahood on this very spot.
The bhikṣus of the Buddha’s era already looked upon it with awe as if facing a vast ocean; how much more so for those of shallow wisdom who came later!
The Venerable Changshui, through his teacherless, spontaneous wisdom, illuminated what was obscure and concealed, dissecting the profound mysteries to provide this commentary.
It is as clear and vivid as seeing the blue sky after parting the clouds and mist; how remarkably brilliant and lucid it is!
Although it was carved into woodblocks for circulation, it has been lost over the years, a source of constant regret for scholars of the Xianshou school.

The layman Shen, seeing this, took pity on him; he searched extensively for excellent manuscripts and completed the transcription in golden script, thereby causing the mani-jewel that had been shattered to become whole once more—truly, one may say he knew how to bestow his bounty.
Does not the Sūtra say: "If there is a single person who gives rise to the true resolve and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all vanish away"?
How could the benefit this brings be anything but profound!
Postscript by the monk De-yun, abbot of Ruiyan, on the Zhonghe Festival in the Jiyou year of the Chunyou era.
